purpose: Investigate whether and when publicly disclosed political activity precedes changes in company government business. No donation-to-contract quid pro quo is inferred.

coverage.caveat: A company's PAC is generally employee-funded; a federal contractor's own federal political contributions can be prohibited. Never add employee, PAC, subsidiary or company spending without distinct, lawfully sourced provenance.

research.headline: About one-third more
research.explanation: Defense contracts obtained by lobbying firms compared with nonlobbying firms, during an unexpected funding increase. The authors explicitly do not identify causation.
research.scope: U.S. federal defense procurement, historical study
research.qualifier: Comparison is about lobbying firms, not every donor or every federal contract.

research.headline: +12.5 percentage points
research.explanation: Estimated increase in likelihood of becoming a federal contractor for firms reporting dark-money contributions, in an observational S&P 500 study. Also +11.8 percentage points for receiving government subsidies.
research.scope: U.S. S&P 500 firm-years, 2008–2022; voluntarily disclosed dark-money giving
research.qualifier: Not a randomized experiment. Disclosure selection and other firm differences can confound.

research.headline: About ¼ standard deviation
research.explanation: An increase in reported donations from $10,000 to $5 million was associated with increased procurement-favoritism risk in a 2004–2015 U.S. federal-contract study.
research.scope: U.S. federal contracts and registered political donations, 2004–2015
research.qualifier: Measures statistical procurement risk, not confirmed corruption or an individual company result.

research.headline: +8–11 percentage points
research.explanation: Prior donations were associated with the chance that the targeted politician later became involved in legislation relevant to donors' lobbying objectives.
research.scope: U.S. federal campaign contributions and lobbying since 1999
research.qualifier: Legislative involvement is not an awarded contract, profits, a vote switch, or a finding of wrongdoing.

cases.status: Two independently sourced activity streams; no proven contract-for-donation path
cases.question: Political spending and awarded government business are both documented. Did one cause the other?

disclosedPolitical.label: Company's published 2024 contributions: subsidiaries plus employee-funded GEO PAC
disclosedPolitical.scope: U.S. federal/national, state/local, and 527 organization contributions; not the same as one FEC committee's spending.

governmentBusiness.scope: 11 registered recipient units including subsidiaries; nominal calendar-year obligated amounts, not revenue, margin or profit.
governmentBusiness.warning: Third-party USAspending compilation not independently reconciled against official award IDs by Power Atlas.

cases.finding: GEO reported 8.6% higher companywide revenue in 2025 ($2.632B vs $2.424B in 2024), and described up to ~$520M in potential incremental annualized revenue from new or expanded 2025 contracts. Meanwhile, a separate USAspending-based aggregation shows lower federal contract obligations in 2025 than 2024. These metrics differ and do not establish that 2024 political spending caused business growth.

companyFinancials.description: The company reported an 8.6% rise in total revenue from 2024 to 2025; three federal customers' share of total revenue rose from 61.8% to 66.6%. Revenue is companywide, not solely federal government contracts.

newBusiness2025.basis: Company-reported potential incremental annualized revenue from new/expanded contracts awarded in 2025; not cash collected or revenue realized in 2025

companyFinancials.caveat: Revenue changes coincide with political spending, public policy changes, operating decisions and government demand. The sources do not show that donations caused the growth.

analyticRules: Only link entities with legal IDs and documented parent/subsidiary relationships; do not use name-only matching as a confirmed ownership or donation link.
Distinguish corporate independent spending, segregated employee-funded PAC giving, company principals' personal giving, lobbying and dark money; never add incompatible categories.
Use date of reported contribution versus decision/award effective date, not merely election year.
Show awards won AND lost, competing bidders, incumbency, contractor size and agency budget before interpreting outcome changes.
Contract obligations are not realized revenue, cash payments, incremental profits or ROI.
Use matched non-donors and pre/post timing as a test; report confounders, uncertainty and negative results. Never label observational associations as quid pro quo.
Respect FEC contributor-data use restrictions and exclude personal addresses/contact information.
